name: Fairness of Depth-Adaptive Early-Exit Inference
statement: Do depth-adaptive / early-exit LLM inference strategies, which allocate compute per token/instance, systematically under-serve specific demographic groups — i.e., do groups exhibit different exit-depth distributions, different accuracy-vs-depth curves, and resulting per-group quality gaps under a fixed exit threshold?
evidence: S7, S8 (fairness surveys, C4); KG cluster C1 open problems
cheapTest: Run a simple threshold-based early-exit (PABEE/FastBERT-style) on a demographic-annotated benchmark (e.g., StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs, BOLD) and measure per-group accuracy, mean exit depth, and the accuracy-vs-depth curve under one fixed threshold; test whether a reliable per-group gap exists.
risk: Early-exit may turn out largely fairness-neutral in practice (small measured effect); per-group quality for open-ended generation is hard to define; confound between group labels and text difficulty could dominate the signal.

name: Group-wise Calibration of the Confidence/Entropy Signal Driving Adaptive Exit
statement: Is the confidence/uncertainty signal (entropy, logit margin) that gates early exit calibrated equally across demographic groups, so a shared threshold exits at the same true-error level for every group — and can per-group calibration (temperature scaling / abstention / selective prediction) make exit decisions group-fair?
evidence: p52, p53, p56, p57 (uncertainty/confidence estimation, C6)
p51, p54, p61 (temperature scaling / universal calibration)
S11 (calibration survey, C6); KG cluster C6 open problems
cheapTest: Compute group-wise ECE/Brier of the exit-confidence signal (output-distribution entropy) across demographic groups on a generation task, then test whether a per-group temperature/calibration mapping reduces the group gap while preserving overall calibration.
risk: Group-wise ECE for open-ended generation is ill-defined and group-specific calibration needs enough per-group data to be stable; risk of over-fitting calibration to small groups or benchmark idiosyncrasies producing a false mitigation.

name: Do Compression and Depth-Budgeting Redistribute Error Onto Minority Groups Through a Shared Mechanism?
statement: Does the mechanism by which model compression (quantization, pruning, distillation) redistributes error onto minority groups transfer to, and help explain, depth-budgeted (early-exit / adaptive-depth) inference — and is there a principled accuracy/efficiency/fairness trade-off curve that exposes it?
evidence: p38 Pruning has a disparate impact on model accuracy
S7, S8 (fairness surveys); KG cluster C5 open problems
cheapTest: On a demographic-annotated dataset, apply one representative pruning method and one quantization method plus an early-exit depth budget; compare per-group accuracy gaps of each against an uncompressed reference to see whether the harmed groups track the same minority groups.
risk: 'Shared mechanism' is a strong causal claim hard to establish cleanly; comparing methods with different compute budgets needs careful Pareto measurement; bias may be dataset-specific and not transfer across compression modes.
